Between the last page of the Old Testament and the first page of the New lie about four hundred years. When the prophet ⟦p:malachi_1899|Malachi⟧ spoke, the Jews who had come home from exile were a small and weary community gathered around a modest rebuilt temple, living quietly as a province of the Persian Empire. When ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s story opens, the same land has a king named ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧, answers to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, speaks Aramaic in its villages and Greek in its cities, and is waiting, with mounting impatience, for God to act. Matthew stands first in the New Testament, and to enter his world we have to cross those silent centuries.

⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧ fell to Alexander the Great of Macedon in the three hundred and thirties before Christ. Alexander died young, but the Greek language and way of life he carried east outlasted him: Greek cities, theatres and gymnasiums, and a common Greek tongue spoken from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ to ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧. His generals divided his empire between them, and ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, caught in the middle, was ruled first by the Ptolemies of Egypt and then by the Seleucid kings of ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧. In Egypt, Jewish scholars translated their Scriptures into Greek, the version later called the Septuagint, and it became the Bible of Jews scattered across the Greek-speaking world.

Under the Seleucid king Antiochus the Fourth, pressure turned to persecution. In the one hundred and sixties before Christ he banned circumcision and the Sabbath and set up a pagan altar in the temple itself. An old priest named Mattathias and his sons rose in revolt, and under Judas, nicknamed Maccabeus, the Hammer, they drove out the Syrian forces and cleansed and rededicated the temple, an event Jews still remember at Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication. Judas's family, the Hasmoneans, became priest-kings, and for about a century the Jews were independent. But the dynasty grew worldly and divided, and in sixty-three before Christ the Roman general Pompey, drawn in to settle a quarrel between two rival brothers, marched into ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ governed through local strongmen, and the strongest was ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧. His family came from ⟦l:edom_357|Idumea⟧, the old land of Edom, and many Jews never fully accepted him. The Roman Senate named him king of the Jews, and he held the throne for more than thirty years. He was a brilliant builder and a brutal ruler. He rebuilt the temple on a magnificent scale, raised the port of ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ and fortresses such as Masada, and put to death a wife and three of his own sons when he suspected them of plotting. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is born in the last years of his reign. When Herod died, Rome divided his kingdom among his sons: ⟦p:archelaus_291|Archelaus⟧ in ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧ in ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and in Perea across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, Philip in the lands to the north-east. Archelaus ruled so badly that Rome soon removed him, and Judea passed to Roman governors, among them ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pontius Pilate⟧.

The religious landscape was crowded. The temple was run by the priests, and the high priest and his council, the Sanhedrin, held real power under ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧. Many of the leading priestly families were Sadducees, conservative aristocrats who accepted only the written law as binding and denied any resurrection of the dead. The Pharisees were a devout and largely lay movement, respected in the towns and villages, who sought to bring the law into every corner of daily life and kept a growing body of oral rules called the tradition of the elders. Scribes, the experts in the law, are often found alongside them. The Essenes withdrew into communities of their own, and the Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran are linked with them. Others dreamed of driving out Rome by the sword. In every town there was a synagogue where the Scriptures were read on the Sabbath, and in many hearts there was a hope for the Messiah, the anointed king from the line of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ who would set Israel free.

The land itself matters. ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ lay in the south, with ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ in its hills. ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ lay in the middle, home to a people whom most Jews avoided. ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ lay in the north, green and fertile and crowded with villages, around a freshwater lake the Gospels call the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧, where fishing was a living. Jerusalem regarded Galilee as provincial, and it is in a Galilean village, ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧, that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ grows up.

The Gospel is the work of ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧, the tax collector whom ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ called to be one of the Twelve, and the church has known it by his name from its earliest days. He wrote for people steeped in the Jewish Scriptures. Matthew quotes the prophets again and again, often with the words this was to fulfil what was spoken, and he usually prefers the phrase kingdom of heaven, in keeping with the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding the name of God.

The book alternates between story and teaching. Five great blocks of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' words stand out, each closing with a phrase like when Jesus had finished saying these things: the Sermon on the Mount, the sending out of the Twelve, the parables of the kingdom, instructions for life among the disciples, and the long discourse on the end of the age. Around them the story moves from the birth in ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧ to the ministry in ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, then to a turning point at ⟦l:caesarea_philippi_267|Caesarea Philippi⟧ when Jesus begins to speak of going to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ to suffer, then south along the road to the city, and into the last week, the Passover, the trial before ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧, the cross and the empty tomb. The Gospel opens with a child to be called Immanuel, God with us, and it closes on a mountain in Galilee with the promise, I am with you always.
1:
⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ begins where any Jewish reader would expect a claim to kingship to begin: with a family tree. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is introduced as the son of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ and the son of ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧, the two men to whom God's great promises were made, and the line runs from one to the other and on down through the kings of Judah to the exile in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ and beyond.

The list is carefully shaped into three sets of fourteen generations, and it holds some surprises. Four women appear besides ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧: ⟦p:tamar_2821|Tamar⟧, Rahab, ⟦p:ruth_2450|Ruth⟧, and ⟦p:uriah_2898|Uriah⟧'s wife, ⟦p:bathsheba_416|Bathsheba⟧, though ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ does not name her. Each has an irregular or foreign story behind her.

Then the birth itself, told from ⟦p:joseph_1715|Joseph⟧'s side. ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧ is pledged to him, a betrothal as binding as marriage, which only a divorce could end, when she is found to be with child. Joseph is a righteous man, unwilling to disgrace her, and he resolves to end the betrothal quietly. An angel speaks to him in a dream, the first of several in these chapters, and the child is given two names, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, which means the Lord saves, and Immanuel, God with us. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ tells this story from Mary's side.
2:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has been born in ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, the small town of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s family a few miles south of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The king on the throne is ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ the Great, now old, suspicious and dangerous, a man who had already killed members of his own family to protect his crown.

Into his capital come the Magi, scholars of the stars from the east. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ does not say how many there were; the tradition of three comes from their three gifts. Their question, where is the one born king of the Jews, could hardly have been put to a worse person.

What follows is a story of rescue and of grief. ⟦p:joseph_1715|Joseph⟧ is again guided by dreams, and the little family escapes to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, which had long been a refuge for Jews in trouble. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ sees in each turn of the story the echo of an older prophecy, and he quotes them one after another. By the last scene, ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ is dead. His son ⟦p:archelaus_291|Archelaus⟧ now rules ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, and Joseph, afraid of him, takes the family north to the obscure Galilean village of ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧.
3:
⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ passes over the years of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' growing up in silence. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ tells us he was about thirty when the next events took place. The scene moves to the wilderness of ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, the barren country falling away toward the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ valley and the Dead Sea, where a new prophet has appeared.

⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧ dresses like ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧, in camel's hair with a leather belt, and he lives on locusts and wild honey. His message is urgent: repent, because the kingdom of heaven is near. Crowds go out from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and all ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ to be baptised by him in the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, confessing their sins. Among them come Pharisees and Sadducees, making their first appearance in the Gospel, and ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧'s words to them are fierce.

⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ speaks of one coming after him, far more powerful. Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ himself arrives from ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and asks to be baptised. John protests, but Jesus insists. As he comes up out of the water, the heavens open, ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ descends like a dove, and a voice from heaven speaks. It is the first time in ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ that God himself speaks, and his words are about who Jesus is.
4:
The voice from heaven has just declared ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ to be God's beloved Son. Now ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ leads him into the wilderness to be tempted by ⟦p:satan_2476|the devil⟧. For forty days and nights he fasts, and the number recalls Israel's forty years in the desert after the exodus. Three times the devil tests him, twice beginning, if you are the Son of God, and three times Jesus answers with words from Deuteronomy, the book of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧' speeches to Israel on the edge of the promised land.

Then the scene shifts north. ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ has been arrested, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ withdraws to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧. He leaves ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧ and settles in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, a fishing town on the north-west shore of the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧, which will become the base for his ministry. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ notes the words of ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ about the land of ⟦p:zebulun_3002|Zebulun⟧ and ⟦p:naphtali_2149|Naphtali⟧, Galilee of the Gentiles, where a great light would dawn.

From that time on, ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ says, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ begins to preach. Beside the lake he calls his first followers, two pairs of fishermen brothers, and by the end of the chapter crowds are gathering from every direction.
5:
The crowds have come from ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, from the ⟦l:decapolis_328|Decapolis⟧ and from beyond the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes up on the mountain and sits down, the usual posture of a Jewish teacher, and his disciples gather close. This is the first of the five great blocks of teaching in ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s Gospel, and it runs through chapter seven. It has come to be called the Sermon on the Mount.

It opens with the Beatitudes, a series of sayings that each begin with the word blessed, and they describe a people quite unlike the powerful and the self-assured. Then he takes up the question his teaching raises: what is his relationship to the Law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧? His answer is that he has come not to abolish it but to fulfil it.

The rest of the chapter is built around a striking refrain. You have heard that it was said, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ begins, and then he quotes the law or a common teaching about it, and adds, but I tell you. He speaks with an authority that does not appeal to any other teacher, and the subjects are close to home: anger, desire, marriage, oaths, revenge, and love for an enemy.
6:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still on the mountainside, and the sermon moves from the law to the practice of devotion. Three things marked a devout Jewish life in his day: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting. Jesus takes each in turn, and each time the contrast is the same, between doing it to be seen by others and doing it for the Father who sees in secret. The hypocrites he describes are, literally, play-actors, the word used for performers on a Greek stage.

At the centre of the chapter, in the section on prayer, is the short prayer ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ gives his disciples, which has been prayed by Christians ever since and is known as the Lord's Prayer. It begins by addressing God as Father.

The second half of the chapter turns to money and worry, matters that touched everyone who heard it in a land of small farmers, fishermen and day labourers. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ draws on the world in front of them, the birds overhead and the wild flowers on the hillside, and he contrasts ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ in all his splendour with the lilies of the field.
7:
This is the final part of the Sermon on the Mount. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ turns to judging others, and the image he chooses comes straight from the carpenter's workshop: a speck of sawdust in a brother's eye, and a whole beam in one's own.

The sayings that follow are short and memorable, among them ask and it will be given, and the rule of doing to others what you would have them do to you. Then the sermon begins to draw to its close with a series of contrasts, each forcing a choice. There are two gates and two roads, two kinds of tree and their fruit, and finally two builders, one who builds on rock and one on sand, in a land where a dry riverbed could become a torrent after a winter storm.

When ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ finishes, the crowds are astonished, ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ says, because Jesus teaches as one who has authority, not as their scribes. The scribes of the day taught largely by citing the opinions of earlier teachers. Jesus has cited no one but Scripture and himself.
8:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ comes down from the mountain, and ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ turns from his words to his deeds. Chapters eight and nine gather a series of miracles, showing the same authority at work that the crowds sensed in the sermon.

The first to come is a man with leprosy, a skin disease that made a person ritually unclean and cut him off from community and worship. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ touches him. Back in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧ a centurion asks for help, a Roman officer and a Gentile, and his understanding of authority amazes Jesus. Then, in ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧'s own house, Peter's mother-in-law is lying ill with a fever.

The chapter moves outward. Would-be followers learn what following will cost. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ and the disciples set out across the lake, which is notorious for sudden, violent storms when the wind drops down from the surrounding hills. On the far side they land in the region of the Gadarenes, on the eastern shore, largely Gentile country, as the herd of pigs makes clear. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ tell this encounter with a single man; ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ tells of two.
9:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ crosses the lake again and returns to ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, which ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ now calls his own town. The miracles continue, but now a new element enters the story: open disagreement. When Jesus tells a paralysed man that his sins are forgiven, some of the scribes say to themselves that this man is blaspheming.

Then comes a call that touches the book itself, because the man concerned is the writer of this Gospel. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ sees a man named ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ sitting at the tax booth and tells him to follow. Tax collectors worked for the authorities, often took more than was due, and were despised as collaborators, and Jesus goes on to eat with a crowd of them. The Pharisees object, and the disciples of ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧ raise a question about fasting.

A run of healings follows: a synagogue leader's daughter who has died, a woman who has suffered bleeding for twelve years, two blind men, and a man unable to speak. The reactions divide. The crowds are amazed. The Pharisees suggest that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ works by the power of the prince of demons. And Jesus, seeing the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, speaks of a harvest that needs workers.
10:
The harvest is plentiful and the workers few, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ now answers his own words. He calls his twelve disciples and sends them out. This is the second of the five blocks of teaching in ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧.

For the first time the twelve are named, as apostles, which means those who are sent. They are listed in pairs: ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon Peter⟧ and ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧, ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, the sons of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧, and the rest, including ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ the tax collector, who had served the authorities, and ⟦p:simon_2746|Simon the Zealot⟧, whose name speaks of fierce zeal. The list ends, ominously, with ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas Iscariot⟧.

Their first mission is limited to the lost sheep of Israel, and they are to travel light, depending on the hospitality of the villages they visit. But as ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes on, his words reach far beyond this first short mission. He speaks of councils and synagogues, governors and kings, of families divided and of disciples hated for his name. The instructions look ahead to a time when following him will be costly in ways the twelve cannot yet imagine.
11:
The twelve have been sent out, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ continues teaching in the towns of ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧. Meanwhile ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧ is in prison, held by ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧; the historian Josephus places him in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. From his cell ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ sends a question, and it is a searching one. Is Jesus really the one who was to come?

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ answers by pointing to what is happening, in words that echo ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧'s pictures of the age to come. Then he speaks to the crowds about ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧, identifying him as the messenger foretold by ⟦p:malachi_1899|Malachi⟧ and the ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ who was to come, the figure whose return Malachi had promised in the very last lines of the Old Testament.

The mood darkens as ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ turns to the towns where most of his miracles have been done, ⟦l:chorazin_299|Chorazin⟧, ⟦l:bethsaida_231|Bethsaida⟧ and ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧ itself, all within a few miles of one another around the northern end of the lake. They have seen his mighty works, and still they have not repented. Yet the chapter closes with one of the gentlest invitations in the Gospels, addressed to the weary and burdened.
12:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has just offered rest to the weary. Now, fittingly, the conflict that has been simmering breaks out over the day of rest itself, the Sabbath. The Pharisees had built up detailed rules about what counted as work on the Sabbath, and plucking ears of grain counted. Jesus answers them from Scripture, with the example of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, and claims a remarkable authority: the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

A healing in a synagogue brings matters to a head, and for the first time ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ records that the Pharisees go out and plot how to kill ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. Jesus withdraws, and Matthew quotes at length from ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧'s song of the gentle servant of the Lord.

The rest of the chapter is a sharp exchange. When ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ heals a blind and mute man, the crowds begin to wonder aloud whether he could be the Son of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, and the Pharisees reply that he drives out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus answers with strong words, and when he is asked for a sign, he points to ⟦p:jonah_1689|Jonah⟧. At the very end his mother and brothers arrive, wanting to speak with him.
13:
On the same day, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes out to the lakeshore. The crowd is so large that he gets into a boat and teaches from the water, while the people stand along the shore. This is the third of ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s five blocks of teaching, and it is made up of parables, short stories drawn from farming, baking, fishing and trade.

The first is the parable of the sower, which ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ later explains to his disciples. In between, they ask him why he speaks to the crowds in parables, and his answer, drawing on ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧, explains much about the division that has opened up in the previous chapters. More parables follow, each opening with the words, the kingdom of heaven is like. An enemy sows weeds among a farmer's wheat. A tiny mustard seed grows into a tree where the birds come to nest. A woman works leaven all through her flour. A man stumbles on treasure hidden in a field, a merchant finds one pearl of great price, and fishermen sort their catch on the shore. Several look to a final separation at the end of the age.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to his hometown, ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧, and teaches in the synagogue. The people there have known him since childhood. They name his mother and his brothers, ⟦p:james_719|James⟧, ⟦p:joseph_1715|Joseph⟧, ⟦p:simon_2747|Simon⟧ and Judas, and they take offence at him.
14:
⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ now brings ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧ into the foreground. He is the son of ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ the Great, and he rules ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and Perea as tetrarch, a lesser title than king, though Matthew also calls him king. Hearing about ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, he tells his servants that this must be ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧, risen from the dead.

That leads ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ to tell, as a flashback, how ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ died. John had condemned ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s marriage to ⟦p:herodias_1507|Herodias⟧, who had been the wife of his brother ⟦p:philip_2345|Philip⟧. The setting is Herod's birthday banquet, and the scene is grim.

When ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ hears the news, he withdraws by boat to a solitary place, but the crowds follow him around the shore. There follows the feeding of the five thousand, the only miracle apart from the resurrection that all four Gospels record. Then Jesus sends the disciples back across the lake while he goes up the mountain alone to pray. Between three and six in the morning, the fourth watch of the night, with the boat struggling against the wind, they see him coming to them on the water. By morning they have landed at ⟦l:gennesaret_458|Gennesaret⟧, on the western shore.
15:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is back on the western shore of the lake, and a delegation of Pharisees and scribes arrives from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, a sign that the authorities in the capital are now taking notice. Their complaint is that his disciples break the tradition of the elders by not washing their hands before eating, a ritual washing rather than a matter of hygiene. Jesus turns the charge back on them and speaks about where defilement really comes from.

Then he leaves Jewish territory altogether and goes north-west to the district of ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧ and ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧, the old Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast. There a Canaanite woman comes to him, crying out for her daughter. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ uses the ancient name for Israel's neighbours, the people of the land before ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, and the exchange that follows is one of the most surprising conversations in the Gospels.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧ and climbs a hillside, and crowds bring their sick to him. Then comes a second feeding, this time of four thousand, in a remote place, after the people have been with him for three days.
16:
The Pharisees, joined now by the Sadducees, two groups who rarely agreed on anything, come to test ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ by asking for a sign from heaven. He refuses, and as the disciples cross the lake he warns them about the leaven of these leaders, a warning they at first misunderstand.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ takes them far to the north, to the region of ⟦l:caesarea_philippi_267|Caesarea Philippi⟧. The city lay at the foot of ⟦l:mount_hermon_841|Mount Hermon⟧, near one of the springs of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, and had been rebuilt by ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s son Philip and named in honour of Caesar. It was a place of pagan shrines and imperial power. There, away from the crowds, Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, and then who they say he is. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ answers.

This is the turning point of the Gospel. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ marks it with the same words he used when ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ began preaching back in chapter four: from that time on. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has just said that many who are first will be last, and the last first.
